newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Superquinn says Tesco's Irish bid a done deal.
newsitem.headline: Superquinn says Tesco's Irish bid a done deal.

text.p: Privately-owned Irish supermarket group Superquinn said on Friday that it had been advised by its lawyers that Tesco's acquisition of ABF's Irish stores was a "done deal".

"It's what they call a Class One test under Stock Exchange regulations. Since it's less than 25 percent of Associated British Foods' assets, they don't have to seek shareholder approval," Superquinn chairman Feargal Quinn told Reuters.
"It looks as though they can close the door and not consider another offer," said Quinn, whose family-owned company had earlier expressed an interest in bidding for the stores.
Earlier, Tesco said it had acquired ABF's food retailing and related businesses in Ireland for 630 million Irish pounds.
Quinn said the only loophole was that the acquisition was subject to EU Commission approval but he was not optimistic about this.
"It's just one British company taking over from another British company," he said.

"We think we've been locked out. We recognise that we were late coming in but we understood negotiations had broken down early yesterday morning and therefore we thought we were going to be given an opportunity."
The group only announced late on Thursday that it was interested in bidding after its financial advisers approached it and said such a bid would be feasible.
Quinn said Superquinn, the smallest of the Irish supermarket chains with 16 shops in the Republic of Ireland, was encouraged that the money was made available to it for a bid.

"I don't think we would have realised that that amount of money was available to a company like ourselves but the high regard in which we've been held by the financial institutions means that we'll now be looking with our eyes open and have more expansionary plans than we otherwise would have had."
Superquinn will now be competing with Tesco in the Irish market.

"We're never relaxed about competition but we believe that the Irish customer, knowing the customer, being close to the customer, will give us a chance to be able to compete more actively than a stranger."
Quinn said Superquinn's participation in a European supermarket buying group of 23,000 should allow it to compete with Tesco after its arrival.
"It's a continuous price war and I can assume that it will be as competitive as ever if not more," he said.
